correctness.rationale: The incidence model uses distinct deletion outputs and distinct codewords, including the single empty output at n=2. Multiplying each output's list constraint by its nonnegative rational weight and each word's upper bound x_w<=1 by its own nonnegative weight gives an upper bound on total code size when each word is covered at weight >=1. Independent exact checks of every entry give the pairs of dual objectives (1,2), (3,9/2), (3,6), (33/5,63/5); taking floors and checking the matching codebooks gives the stated exact shorter-length capacities. The length-six compatibility graph on 729 words uses disjoint shadows as adjacency, so unique-decoding codes are its cliques. An independent Python reproduction greedily colors candidate prefixes into independent classes, searches include/exclude extensions with safe color pruning, and returns maximum 11 after 1,428,176 nodes (tested first at n=5, maximum 6). The checked size-11 and size-24 codebooks have shadow loads at most one and two, respectively. Since 24>22 and all shorter lengths satisfy the required non-strict inequality, the first strict gap is proved; the exact length-six list-two capacity is not determined. value.rationale: The factor two is the natural benchmark since any union of two unique codes is list-two and has size at most twice the unique capacity. Proving strict separation for the first length, with exact earlier capacities and an explicit witness exceeding that benchmark, answers a meaningful finite coding question. This is not just a recollection of short unique-decoding tables and does not require determining the exact length-six list-two optimum.
